analysis.title: US Economics Analyst: 2027 Capex Outlook: How Much of an AI Boost?
key_insights: Real business fixed investment grew at an 11% annualized rate in 2026Q1-Q3, and GS expects 8.4% in Q4. AI spending accounted for about 6.5pp of overall business fixed investment growth this year.

Investment tax incentives in last year's fiscal bill likely added about 3pp to capex growth in 2026, more than offsetting a modest drag from falling manufacturing facility construction as IRA and CHIPS Act subsidies faded.

GS estimates AI-related hardware and IP spending will exceed $900bn annualized by end-2026 (about $800bn on hardware, a $550bn increase from 2025) and reach $1.4tn by end-2027 ($1.3tn on hardware, a further $500bn increase), roughly 4% of US GDP. The 2027 increase is expected to be frontloaded, with growth slowing somewhat in 2H27.

AI's measured impact is smaller than headline spending for three reasons: real AI spending grows only $250-300bn (about 0.8% of GDP) because computer and semiconductor prices are rising strongly, most AI equipment is imported and netted out of GDP, and GDP statistics treat semiconductors as intermediate inputs rather than investment.

Imported semiconductors used for AI make a negative contribution to measured GDP, because they are counted as imports but not as investment. Only a small share of US chip design value added has been captured as exports of technology services.
AI-related spending is estimated to boost true capex growth by 5.3pp in 2027 but measured capex growth by only 4.3pp.

Direct effects of AI investment add 0.2pp to measured real GDP growth in both 2026 and 2027. True GDP impact is 0.8pp in 2026 and 0.7pp in 2027 after adding unmeasured chip investment and chip design exports. Including indirect spillovers, AI boosts real GDP growth by 0.6pp in both years.

Indirect AI effects include a consumer spending boost from stock market wealth effects, a hit to real income from higher electricity and other prices caused by AI demand, and limited crowding out of other spending.

GS expects newly elected Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia and Michigan, which account for over a third of planned US data center capacity, to impose data center moratoria. The moratoria will likely hit only projects not yet permitted, so the vast majority of planned 2027 construction is unaffected.

GS gives three reasons moratoria should not disrupt 2027: they cover only unpermitted projects, spending is concentrated in the back half of the 2-3-year construction timeline, and moratoria are not expected to be long-lived. Stricter or longer-lasting moratoria are a downside risk, particularly in 2028-2029.

Declining construction of IRA and CHIPS Act-subsidized manufacturing facilities cut capex growth by 0.5pp in 2026 and is expected to subtract 0.4pp in 2027. Equipment spending to outfit factories and data centers nearing completion should partly offset this, and industrial equipment investment is likely to remain strong.

Energy investment should add to capex growth. Higher oil prices since the start of the Iran war added 0.5pp to capex growth in 2026, and GS expects another 0.5pp in 2027, though producers are prioritizing capital discipline over production growth.

GS commodity strategists estimate WTI must stay above $70/barrel (vs roughly $90 today) for US producers to keep raising capex. A quick end to the war with a sharp oil price decline would make the energy contribution smaller or negative.

Financial conditions have tightened notably over the past two months, led by higher rates and lower equity prices. GS's FCI impulse framework implies a 1.0pp drag on 2027 capex growth if the FCI stays at today's level. The drag would be larger if rates keep rising and equities keep falling, and smaller if strategists' forecasts of lower long-term rates, higher equities and a weaker dollar materialize.
GS forecasts 2027 real business fixed investment growth of 8% Q4/Q4, versus consensus of 4.2%, with a very slight deceleration over the year. GS forecasts 2027 real GDP growth of 2.4% Q4/Q4.

tension_points.bull_case: AI-related spending reaches $1.4tn annualized by end-2027 (about 4% of GDP), adding 5.3pp to true capex growth and 0.6pp to true GDP growth, which supports GS's 8% capex forecast versus 4.2% consensus.
tension_points.bear_case: The measured effect is much smaller: 4.3pp on capex and 0.2pp on GDP, because most AI equipment is imported and netted out, semiconductors are not counted as investment, and rising chip prices cut real growth.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Stricter or longer-lasting data center moratoria in Texas, Georgia and Michigan, particularly in 2028-2029.

tension_points.bull_case: Higher oil prices since the Iran war began added 0.5pp to capex growth in 2026, and GS expects another 0.5pp in 2027.
tension_points.bear_case: Producers keep prioritizing capital discipline over production growth, and a quick end to the war with sharply lower oil would shrink or reverse the contribution.

tension_points.bull_case: Strategists forecast lower long-term interest rates, higher equity prices and a weaker dollar, which would reduce the drag on capex.
tension_points.bear_case: Financial conditions have tightened notably over the past two months, and at the current FCI level the drag on 2027 capex growth is 1.0pp, larger if rates keep rising and equities keep falling.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Continued rises in interest rates and falls in equity prices beyond today's FCI level.
